headline: Here’s why your pay raise still leaves you feeling broke
author: Michelle Singletary

paragraphs.text: “I hate payday.”
Who dislikes the day they get paid for all their work?
Yet over the years, as I’ve sat across the table from individuals and couples trying to stretch their income, I’ve heard variations of that same disheartening line.
“I hate it because all my money is gone as soon as it hits my bank account,” one guy told me during a financial meeting in which I was trying to help him and his wife balance their budget.
The feeling he described is the reality for millions of households: mounting debt payments make it hard to save for emergencies, invest for retirement or achieve other financial goals.

You expect necessities — housing, transportation and food — to take up much of your pay. But non-mortgage debt (credit cards, auto loans and student loans) is steadily consuming an increasing share of what remains.

A new report reveals that, for the average worker since late 2022, debt payments have risen 14.8 percent, compared with 1.7 percent real income growth, meaning the debt people are servicing has grown eight times faster than real take-home pay, according to the Century Foundation, a progressive think tank, and Protect Borrowers, an advocacy group focused on consumer debt.

About 80 percent of working-age adults carry consumer debt, with required monthly payments claiming roughly 10 percent of after-tax household income, up from 8.9 percent at the end of 2022. Credit cards and auto loans drive nearly all of this burden, accounting for 44 percent and 40 percent of monthly debt obligations, respectively.

For a single earner, real monthly take-home pay has risen by an average of $109 since late 2022, while required monthly debt payments have increased by $57. This means 52 cents of every dollar in wage gains was absorbed by non-mortgage debt service before it could be spent on basic necessities or used to build a savings cushion.

In a dual-earner household where both partners experienced the average increase in debt payments, their combined monthly debt obligations rose by $114, outpacing their total household real income gain of $109. As a result, 100 percent (and then some) of the household’s net income gain was wiped out by rising debt obligations.

“For the average family, it really feels like we’re on the precipice of a cliff where they’re trying to manage their finances with this kind of Jenga of different types of debt,” Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the Century Foundation, said in an interview. “The rest of the economy is humming along almost without them buoyed by AI stocks.”
Without adequately considering the liabilities side of a household’s budget, “conventional measures of real earnings increasingly understate workers’ financial insecurity,” the report notes.
With the midterm elections less than a month away, affordability is on the minds of many voters. The analysis raises an important question: Is your wage growth largely an illusion?
To emphasize the drag debt has on household finances, the two organizations propose a new economic metric: Real Income Net of Debt (RIND).
The goal is to force policymakers to confront the extent to which debt is precariously propping up American households, Margetta Morgan said.

I’ve often heard critics characterize consumer debt as the result of reckless or unnecessary spending. But the data disputes that narrative. The reality is many households are turning to debt to afford the basics, such as groceries and gas.

“There are these stereotypes that debt is some kind of frivolous spending,” Margetta Morgan said. “It is absolutely unfair. What we see time and again is people making pretty rational choices ... People are putting their basic expenses onto credit cards.”

When government safety nets pull back, families have no choice but to borrow to bridge the gap. Millions of Americans, including more than a million children, have lost access to federal food assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), according to an analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a progressive policy organization.

At the same time, about one-third of Americans — roughly 82 million people — say they have had to make financial sacrifices, cutting back on essentials like food and utilities to cover health care expenses, according to findings from the West Health-Gallup Affordability Index.
“Families are increasingly relying on consumer debt to build their own safety nets,” Margetta Morgan said.
Auto loans are also straining family budgets. A monthly car payment that includes a comma is the new normal for an increasing number of borrowers.

A record 21.2 percent of new-car buyers took out $1,000-plus monthly loans in the third quarter of 2026, borrowing an average of $44,664, according to recent data from Edmunds, a car-shopping website. The average new-car payment rose to $787, up from $756 a year earlier.
Used-car shoppers aren’t escaping the squeeze either. The average payment was $582 on $30,703 in debt, pushing a record 6.5 percent of used-car buyers into four-figure monthly payments.

Debt taken on for basic necessities disproportionately impacts working-class families, the report said. Monthly credit card and auto payments are surprisingly similar across income tiers, but lower-income earners pay far higher interest rates for less valuable goods.
“It is much more expensive to be poor in this country, and as a result, it’s also much harder to climb out of that kind of mountain of debt,” Margetta Morgan said.

For millions of working families, student debt adds another layer of burden. Student loans currently account for just 7.5 percent of total consumer debt payments, a share that could rise as more borrowers face higher monthly payments due to recent policy changes, according to findings from the Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers.

This burden is even heavier when systemic inequities are factored in. Among prime borrowers with top-tier credit scores, Black workers spend 13.6 percent of their take-home income on consumer debt service, compared to 8.4 percent for White workers.

“Black workers have to achieve a higher level of postsecondary education to get the same wages as a White worker,” Margetta Morgan said. “Right from the get-go, you’re adding to your debt burden even just to get the wages that other workers would get.”
Traditional economic metrics measure affordability by looking at wages and prices. But that leaves out the hidden siphon draining family budgets every month: debt.
Workers are losing ground as prices outstrip paychecks. When required debt service is factored in, net earnings drop even further.

Wages, inflation and debt form an economic trio that provides a fuller picture of a household’s financial well-being. Taken together, these factors explain why families feel broke in an economy that looks good on paper. The affordability crisis isn’t a hoax or a phony talking point. It’s real people looking at their bank accounts and realizing the math simply isn’t mathing.
